profiles.meeting_scenario: At a tertiary pediatric medical center, the audiology service and speech-language pathology service are holding a coordination meeting to prepare the parent-facing workflow for a newly adopted interdisciplinary care coordination model in the pediatric hearing clinic. The clinic is transitioning away from a one-day multidisciplinary assessment format after parent feedback showed that families felt overwhelmed, were unclear about which disciplines were involved, and wanted better information about functional hearing in daily life. The meeting agenda is to align on the shared parent summary packet, the handoff from same-day clinical visits to follow-up outreach, and how each service will update the care coordinator about what has already been explained to families. The expected outcome is an agreed plan for what each discipline contributes to the parent summary, when the care coordinator contacts the family, and what counts as the visit being ready for handoff.

members.name: Dr. Lena Morales
members.role: Pediatric Audiologist and Hearing Clinic Workstream Lead
members.expertise: Diagnostic audiology, pediatric hearing technology, multidisciplinary clinic operations
members.background: Dr. Morales has worked for eight years in a tertiary pediatric hearing center and is leading implementation changes after the parent-experience review; she is accustomed to coordinating testing results, device discussions, and referrals across same-day clinic encounters.
members.private_state: She wants the new process to reduce repeat parent questions to audiology after clinic and to show leadership that the transition to interdisciplinary coordination is already operational without adding major documentation burden to her team.
hidden_assumptions: A 'parent summary' is a concise after-visit document families take home the same day, not a later synthesized note.
If functional hearing is 'covered,' that means audiology has discussed listening implications in classroom and home settings during counseling around test results and amplification.

Once audiology uploads the finalized hearing results and recommendation sheet into the shared chart, the case is effectively ready for care-coordinator follow-up unless a physician-specific order is pending.
The 'one-week follow-up' means outreach within five business days after the clinic date, consistent with service operations reporting.

members.name: Erin Patel
members.role: Pediatric Speech-Language Pathologist and Family Care Coordination Liaison
members.expertise: Early communication intervention, caregiver counseling, interdisciplinary family education
members.background: Erin supports speech-language evaluations in the hearing clinic and was asked to help redesign family communication after qualitative parent feedback highlighted confusion about provider roles and next steps.
members.private_state: She wants a parent-facing process that clearly distinguishes disciplines, gives families digestible explanations after the visit, and ensures no family is contacted before all disciplines' recommendations are integrated into one coherent plan.
hidden_assumptions: A 'parent summary' is an integrated cross-discipline plain-language document that may be finalized after the visit once all recommendations are reconciled.

Functional hearing information is only truly 'covered' if families receive explicit examples about listening in social, classroom, and everyday communication contexts, not just counseling tied to test results.
A case is not ready for handoff until speech-language, audiology, and physician recommendations have all been reconciled into a single coordinated message for the family.
The 'one-week follow-up' means by the next calendar week so families are not left waiting through a weekend or scheduling gap.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to finalize the 'parent summary' for families.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a same-day after-visit summary packet containing audiology results, immediate next steps, and discipline-specific inserts that can go home before the family leaves clinic.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a later integrated family summary written in plain language after all disciplines have aligned, even if that is sent 1-2 days after the visit.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In clinical settings, 'summary' naturally sounds shared and uncontroversial; both want parents to receive a summary, so neither thinks to unpack timing, format, or whether it is discipline-specific versus integrated.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as covering functional hearing
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the new workflow should make sure 'functional hearing is covered.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this is satisfied if audiology counseling connects the audiogram and device recommendations to likely listening performance at home and school during the visit.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this is satisfied only if families are given explicit, structured examples and written explanation about social and academic listening demands in everyday life, separate from technical results counseling.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both endorse the same parent-feedback lesson and use the same improvement language, but their threshold for what counts as adequate coverage differs in a way that sounds like nuance rather than disagreement.

misalignment_points.topic: Readiness for handoff to care coordination
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss when a case is 'ready for handoff' to the care coordinator.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes handoff readiness refers to the audiology workstream being complete enough for the coordinator to schedule outreach and reinforce recommendations, even if other disciplines add details later.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes handoff readiness includes a fully reconciled interdisciplinary plan with all disciplines' recommendations and provider-role explanations already consolidated.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Coordination meetings routinely use 'handoff' as if it were a single operational milestone; each person sees their interpretation as the obvious clinic-safe boundary, so the scope difference stays invisible.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree families should get 'one-week follow-up.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects the coordinator to complete outreach within five business days after the appointment, matching internal turnaround expectations and allowing time for chart finalization.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects outreach by the next calendar week, often within 3-7 calendar days, because the family experience issue is perceived as delay and uncertainty rather than internal turnaround.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'one-week follow-up' is standard operational shorthand that usually goes unexamined; both hear it as prompt contact and do not think to specify business versus calendar days.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to sound streamlined and already workable. If families leave clinic with clear next steps in hand, we should cut down on the follow-up calls that keep bouncing back to audiology. And if we can frame this as tightening what we're already doing, leadership will see the interdisciplinary model as operational without my team taking on a big extra documentation project.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I think the main goal today is to tighten the new interdisciplinary workflow so families leave the hearing clinic visit with clearer next steps and we have a more consistent process across the team.

turns.inner_thought: The parent interviews were very clear: families felt flooded with information, didn't always know who was saying what, and they especially did not feel functional hearing was covered in a way that connected to daily communication. I want us to build something parent-facing that separates provider roles but still lands as one coherent message.
turns.utterance: Yes, and the parent feedback gives us a pretty strong anchor. Families said they felt overwhelmed, they weren't always sure which discipline was providing care, and they especially wanted us to make sure functional hearing is covered in a way that feels meaningful in daily life.

turns.inner_thought: For me the parent summary should be the concise packet they leave with that day—results, immediate recommendations, inserts as needed. If that's finalized before checkout, the coordinator can use it right away and we avoid the usual post-visit confusion. Also, once audiology has uploaded finalized results and recommendations, the case is basically ready for handoff unless there's some physician order still pending.
turns.utterance: From the clinic operations side, I'd like us to finalize the parent summary for every family before checkout. That way the care coordinator has something consistent to reference, and we're not relying on families to piece the visit together afterward.

turns.inner_thought: Absolutely, the parent summary is the core deliverable. I mean the integrated family document that goes out once audiology, speech, and physician recommendations are reconciled into one plain-language plan. As long as it reflects a single coordinated message, families won't get separate threads from each service.
turns.utterance: I agree completely that the parent summary is essential. I think the big thing is that it needs to reflect a single coordinated message across audiology, speech, and the physician team so it reads as one plan for the family.

turns.inner_thought: Audiology can definitely own the hearing results section. We already explain what the test findings mean and connect them to listening at home and school when we talk through amplification and recommendations, so that should satisfy making sure functional hearing is covered. I don't want to create a whole separate counseling workflow if we can just capture what we're already doing.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. Audiology can own the section on hearing results, and during result counseling and device discussion we can make sure functional hearing is covered so the family has that context alongside the recommendations.

turns.inner_thought: Good. But I still want a brief family-friendly page that gives explicit examples of listening demands in everyday settings, because to me that's what it means for functional hearing to be covered consistently. If it's folded into the parent summary, families will actually have something to revisit at home and it won't depend on how they interpreted the technical counseling in the room.
turns.utterance: That works well. I can help draft a brief family-friendly page with examples from social and academic listening so functional hearing is covered consistently for every family.

turns.inner_thought: Operationally, I want the trigger to be simple: once audiology test results and the recommendation sheet are in the chart, the coordinator should be able to move. We can't hold outreach waiting for every discipline to polish language if the core information is already there. The faster that handoff starts, the fewer parent questions circle back to us.
turns.utterance: On the handoff piece, I think once the test results and recommendations are in the chart, the case should be ready for handoff to the care coordinator. That gives us a clear operational point to move the family into follow-up.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, handoff is exactly the bridge we need—but only once the family message is pulled together across disciplines. I don't want the coordinator contacting parents with partial information and then having to revise it when speech or physician recommendations are added. If the parent summary is truly one message, handoff will feel much cleaner.
turns.utterance: I like having that handoff point. It should really help once the family message is pulled together, because then parents aren't hearing separate pieces from each discipline after the visit.

turns.inner_thought: We should lock in one-week follow-up as the standard—within five business days is realistic for the coordinator and aligns with service reporting. That gives enough time for chart finalization but still feels prompt. It also lets the coordinator reinforce referrals and answer device questions instead of those calls landing back with audiology.
turns.utterance: For timing, I'd suggest we set one-week follow-up as the standard. The coordinator can use that contact to check parent understanding, confirm referrals, and catch device questions that come up after clinic.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, one-week follow-up is exactly right, meaning families should hear from us by the next calendar week so they aren't sitting through a weekend wondering what happens next. The visit needs to stay fresh, especially if they left with a lot to process. If we wait too long, confusion grows and the coordinated message loses impact.
turns.utterance: I agree on one-week follow-up. Families should hear from the coordinator quickly while the visit is still fresh and before confusion sets in.

turns.inner_thought: So the plan is straightforward from my side: audiology builds the parent summary template, we include language on functional hearing within our existing counseling flow, and once our documentation is complete we trigger ready for handoff. That should be enough structure to show this process is live without adding a whole second layer of charting.
turns.utterance: Okay, so my understanding is that audiology will prepare the parent summary template, include the functional hearing language, and trigger handoff after documentation is complete.

turns.inner_thought: Great. I'll shape the family-friendly wording so the parent summary reads as one integrated plan, and I'll connect that to the coordinator's one-week follow-up so families get a coherent explanation rather than separate discipline updates. This is the piece that can really fix the role confusion parents described.
turns.utterance: That sounds good. I'll draft the family-friendly wording, align it with the coordinator's one-week follow-up process, and make sure the parent summary reads as one plan for the family.
